questions.question: What does a contamination check in the data pipeline verify?
options: That training data does not contain malware or adversarial examples
That no training or validation examples overlap with held-out benchmark test sets, using MinHash similarity
That PII tokens have been removed from the dataset by Presidio
That deduplication has reduced the raw corpus to under 300k examples
questions.explanation: A MinHash-based contamination check compares every split against MMLU-Pro, MT-Bench-v2, and RewardBench-2 test sets, rejecting any overlapping examples that would inflate benchmark scores.

questions.question: What is GRPO and how does it differ from DPO?
options: GRPO uses human preference pairs ranked by annotators; DPO uses model-generated preference pairs
GRPO is DeepSeek R1's RL recipe using verifiable rewards (e.g., math/code correctness); DPO uses labeled preference pairs without a reward model
GRPO fine-tunes only the attention layers; DPO updates all parameters
GRPO runs on a single GPU; DPO requires at least 8xH100
questions.explanation: GRPO (Group-Relative Policy Optimization) is DeepSeek R1's RL recipe where the reward is verifiable (e.g., math answer is correct). DPO optimizes directly on preference pairs without requiring explicit reward model training.

questions.question: What does the EAGLE-3 acceptance rate measure, and why does it matter for throughput?
options: The fraction of training tokens that survive the quality filter
The fraction of drafted tokens the target model accepts without resampling; higher rates mean more tokens advance per verify pass, increasing throughput
The fraction of MMLU-Pro questions the quantized model answers correctly
The ratio of FP8 weights to FP16 weights in the served model
questions.explanation: EAGLE-3 draft heads propose k tokens per step; the target model verifies them all in one pass. The acceptance rate is the fraction of drafted tokens accepted, directly determining how many tokens are generated per GPU cycle and thus throughput.

questions.question: Why does the pipeline produce three quantization formats (GPTQ-INT4-Marlin, AWQ-INT4, GGUF-Q4_K_M) rather than one?
options: Different formats are required for different cloud providers
Each format targets a different deployment scenario: Marlin for GPU throughput, AWQ for balanced inference, GGUF for llama.cpp on CPU/edge
MOF 2026 mandates that all three formats be published in the model card
The three formats are used at different training stages: SFT, DPO, and GRPO respectively
questions.explanation: GPTQ-Marlin is optimized for GPU throughput, AWQ provides a balanced GPU option, and GGUF-Q4_K_M enables inference on CPU or edge hardware via llama.cpp. Different use cases warrant different quant formats.

questions.question: What is the Model Openness Framework (MOF) and what must a 2026-compliant model card include?
options: A Hugging Face hub template requiring an accuracy table and license field
The 2026 standard grading model releases on data, training code, eval, safety, license, and reproducibility (with YAMLs and commit SHAs)
An Anthropic internal document for publishing closed-weight models
A legal framework for determining whether model weights can be exported internationally
questions.explanation: MOF 2026 is a standard that grades open model releases on completeness: data description, training code, evaluation results, safety testing, licensing, and a reproducibility section with configs and commit hashes.

questions.question: Which evaluation benchmarks does the capstone use to compare SFT-only vs SFT+DPO vs SFT+GRPO?
options: GLUE, SQuAD, and HellaSwag
lm-evaluation-harness tasks including MMLU-Pro, MT-Bench-v2, and RewardBench-2
SWE-bench Verified, HumanEval, and MBPP
GSM8K, ARC-Challenge, and WinoGrande
questions.explanation: The capstone's eval matrix runs lm-evaluation-harness, RewardBench-2, MT-Bench-v2, and MMLU-Pro across all four checkpoints (base, SFT-only, SFT+DPO, SFT+GRPO) to measure the gain from each stage.
